paras: The shooting of Wayman Booker was an attack on a resident of Shamrock, Kentucky, by four white men on a drunken spree, reported in a dispatch dated June 13, 1919. Booker was shot four times in the abdomen and described as fatally wounded, and the men escaped with no reward offered for their capture. The Chicago Defender carried the only known report, on its front page.

Booker was described as "a prominent resident" of Shamrock and as "well known in secret order circles." His race is not stated in the report, though the Defender's framing of the story around his white attackers implies he was Black.

According to the Shamrock dispatch, four white men "on a drunken spree" shot Booker, and four bullets entered his abdomen. No reason for the shooting and no prior encounter between Booker and the men is described. Booker was taken to the hospital in Middlesbrough, where at the time of the report he was on the operating table.
The men escaped, and the Defender noted that no reward had been offered for their capture. No report of Booker's death, of arrests, or of an inquest appears in the coverage found.

The Chicago Defender ran the story on June 14, 1919, as a short front-page item under the headline "Whites on Spree Shoot." The item named the attackers by race, emphasized Booker's standing in the town, and closed its account of the shooting by pointing out that the men had escaped and no reward was offered. It shared a column block with an unrelated Hopkinsville, Kentucky, item about the appointment of the editor Phil H. Brown, and no follow-up appeared in the Black papers searched.
